The third is that trial court's interpretation below contradicts District Court and Florida Supreme Court interpretations of that statute, although it has not been directly addressed under the type of fact scenario here, and that it departs from the plain language of the statute, that the trial court's interpretation actually eviscerates the PIP statute, the purpose of the particular sections that we're here to talk about, and the legal opinion cited by the trial court are distinguishable and improperly read as an exception to the statute. We're gonna have to go back a little bit into the history of the Personal Injury Protection Statute, and I know the Fifth District in particular has been wading into those waters pretty deeply of late, but in this particular section, they put in there what was a 30-day requirement for providers to submit bills, and then they expanded it in 2001 to 35 days, and we're gonna talk about that migration, but there was a reason why they put it in, and that reason is discussed by the Fourth Supreme Court, by the way, in a case called Warren versus State Farm, which they took up the Supreme Court, and from the Fifth District Court of Appeal on several issues, and predominantly focusing on constitutionality, which is not an issue before the court today. But what the purpose of this particular section of having providers submit their bills within a stated time limit before, again, 30 days, now 35 days, is multiple. The first one, as cited by the courts, is to avoid bulk billing, and you'll go, what does bulk billing have to do with the 35-day requirement? And it's this, what used to happen is there would be a holdback of medical bills, and there was a holdback for a couple of reasons, and that is if a provider had what I would characterize as a multidisciplinary clinic with osteopaths, chiropractic physicians, medical doctors, and so on, as the statute was at the time, you had to have an IME within 30 days by doctors or physicians under each of those licensing chapters in order to suspend benefits. And so what would happen is they'd hold back these bills, they'd bulk bill, and boom, they'd hit them all at one time by these multidisciplinary clinics, and then it was a challenge for them to get IMEs from all of the doctors in all of those disciplines. The second thing had to do with the deductible, and so if you had bills, you would hold back, hold back, hold back your bills, and then the deductible would be expended by somebody else, and then you would submit your bills and not get hit by the deductible. There were other challenges or other reasons to do it, and that is that the insurance policies and the insurance companies have certain investigative powers, which are actually, again, part of the PIP statute. One is independent medical examinations, and the other is examinations under oath. I'm sure it won't come as a great shock to the court, but since the early or late 1990s and early 2000s, there have been issues with PIP medical providers regarding medical abuse, medical fraud, and so on, and so those investigative tools were very important. In fact, in the most recent version of the statute from 2012, they put in a 14-day rule, since you have to come on a treater's radar and ultimately on the insurer's, PIP insurer's radar within 14 days so that bills would be payable. So this is what they put in the statute. Originally, it says, with respect to, and I mentioned the two exceptions, with respect to any treatment or service other than medical services billed by a hospital or provider for emergency services, that's exception number one, as defined by 395.002, or inpatient services rendered at a hospital, the statement of charges must be furnished to the insurer by the provider.
